subtitle: Plan continuity around critical work, share knowledge through accessible practice, and create voluntary mentoring relationships with clear responsibilities and limits.
audience: For experienced supervisors, managers and senior leaders who want critical knowledge to outlast any one person, and who are open to learning from colleagues earlier in their careers or with different backgrounds.

lessons.title: Continuity is about functions, not favorites
objectives: Map one critical function in your area that depends on knowledge held by a single person.
Distinguish a continuity review of a function from naming a preferred successor.
Describe how relying on one person can limit who gets a fair chance to learn the work.
Identify which continuity decisions belong with Human Resources or labor relations.
lessons.teaching:
A team may have critical work whose practical knowledge is concentrated in one person. It might be the history behind a provider agreement, the steps for a federal report, or knowing which county contact to call when a payment stalls. When that person retires, changes jobs or takes leave, gaps in coverage can delay work and affect the people who depend on it. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's Succession Planning Process guidance asks leaders to find the real continuity issues and to plan around long-term talent needs rather than one-for-one replacement of positions.

Start with the function, not the person. Succession planning asks who could develop toward a role; a continuity review asks what the work needs and how many people could do it. Ask what must keep working, what knowledge it depends on, where that knowledge lives today and how many people could do it next month. Write the answers as tasks, decisions, contacts and documents. Include the quieter parts too: yearly deadlines, workarounds and the relationships that keep it running. Leave out who the heir should be, and do not rate anyone's readiness. For this learning exercise, describe the function without rating possible successors. A document’s shareability depends on its information and access rules, not whether it would embarrass someone. Keep restricted operational information in authorized systems.

A single point of knowledge is also an equity question. Informal learning may be easier to access for people who share a location or schedule with the experienced colleague. Check the actual opportunities available to remote or part-time staff and to people with access needs, rather than assuming who has been included. The same OPM guidance describes building pools of people from several levels, starting early in careers, instead of developing one person for one position. Ask who has had a real chance to learn this work, whose interest has never been asked about, and how you would find out.

Some continuity decisions are not yours to make alone. A function review is a planning and learning tool. Follow agency hiring, assignment and classification procedures, and consult Human Resources or labor relations when a proposed change affects their responsibilities. A learning plan does not authorize an appointment or change a labor agreement. Bring them the function gap you found and ask what options exist. Keep this exercise focused on functions and knowledge. Authorized workforce planning may also require individual records or assessments; use the approved process for that work instead of converting this exercise into an informal selection list.
lessons.keyPoint: Identify the functions and knowledge needed for continuity, then broaden access to learning. Follow the authorized process for appointments, assignments and classification decisions.
lessons.example: Practice case: Imani manages a waiver policy team in the division. Doug, a policy lead, is the only person who fully understands how waiver amendments move through review, and he plans to retire next year. Reuben, a deputy director, asks Imani to name Doug's replacement by Friday so training can start. Imani knows two other staff have asked to learn amendment work and neither has been offered it. She is not sure what Reuben's request commits her to.
lessons.question: What should Imani do first?
choices: Name the senior analyst who already helps Doug most weeks, since that person knows the most and training could begin right away.
Map the amendment work with Doug, open the learning to several interested staff, and ask Human Resources about any formal assignment.
Ask Doug to spend his remaining months writing a complete manual of the process, so the knowledge is saved and nobody has to be chosen for now.
feedback: This is quick and the analyst may be capable. It also settles who learns the work by proximity, before anyone has looked at what the function needs or who else wants to learn it.
This is the recommended choice. It keeps the focus on the function, gives interested staff a fair chance to learn, and leaves any formal assignment with the people who decide it.
A written record helps, but much of Doug's judgment will not reach a manual written alone. Without people learning alongside him, the team still depends on one source of knowledge.
lessons.reflection: Which parts of your own work would stall if you were away for a month? How would someone on your team get a real chance to learn them today?
lessons.action: Choose one function in your area that depends on one person. Write a half-page review of it: the main steps, the decisions, the contacts and the documents. Leave out the names of any possible successors.

check.question: What makes a continuity review different from naming a successor?
check.correct: It describes the tasks, decisions and knowledge a function needs, without choosing a person.
wrong: It lists the people most ready to take over the function, in order of their experience.
It records each employee's current skills so leaders can compare people over time.
check.feedback: This exercise maps a function without selecting a successor. Individual assessment and selection may be legitimate parts of authorized workforce planning, but they require the applicable agency process.

lessons.title: Making tacit knowledge shareable for everyone
objectives: Choose a mix of shadowing, side-by-side work and written guides to share one piece of working knowledge.
Draft a plain-language handoff note that someone new to the task can use on their own.
Adapt a knowledge-sharing plan for different access needs, schedules and languages.
Check whether knowledge has transferred by having the learner do the task and explain it.
lessons.teaching:
Much of what experienced people know is never written down. It shows up as judgment: which provider call to return first, why a letter is worded a certain way, which lead-agency role is responsible for answering a particular question. People often cannot list this knowledge until they are doing the work, and they may not see it as knowledge at all; to them it is just how the job is done. A manual can preserve important information, but practice and discussion help reveal judgments or exceptions that the writer may not think to explain.

Use more than one way to share working knowledge. OPM's Succession Planning Process guidance lists methods such as shadowing, coaching and mentoring, action learning projects and communities of practice, and OPM's mentoring guidance names knowledge transfer as one reason agencies set up mentoring. A practical sequence is to watch, then work side by side, then do the task while the expert reviews. Then the learner, not the expert, writes or updates the guide. Writing it in their own words shows what they understood and what they missed. Where you can, teach two people, so the knowledge does not move from one single point to another.

Design the handoff for the people who will use it. Ask who will learn the work and what they need to take part. Shadowing that only happens in person at seven in the morning leaves out a colleague on a different schedule or working remotely. Recorded walkthroughs need captions. Written guides need clear headings that a screen reader can follow, plain language and defined terms. A colleague working in a second language may want written steps and a short glossary, and others learn best by talking it through. Ask rather than assume. A possible accommodation request does not require special wording. Follow the agency process and promptly forward it to the appropriate decision maker if that is not your role. Accessible design should also be part of routine planning.

Judge success by the work, not the document. A demonstration of the task and its key decisions gives better evidence of readiness than the existence of a guide alone. Use an authorized practice setting, relevant assistive tools and any required supervision; one demonstration does not prove readiness for every exception. Ask what was unclear and revise. Plan a check-in a few weeks after the handoff, when real questions have come up. Keep the guide with the function in a shared place, with a date and the role responsible for updating it. The aim is to check the handoff, not to grade the learner.
lessons.keyPoint: Working knowledge moves through watching, doing together and doing with review. Shape each step around the people learning, and judge it by whether they can do the work.
lessons.example: Practice case: Tomas supervises a unit that supports county eligibility staff. Folasade, a senior specialist, starts a six-month leave next month, and she alone handles the annual reconciliation, mostly by phone with county partners. Tomas has planned two weeks of in-office shadowing for Kwame and Ana. Kwame works a compressed schedule and is remote two days a week. Ana is hard of hearing and relies on captions for calls. Tomas wants both of them ready.
lessons.question: How should Tomas set up the handoff?
choices: Ask Kwame and Ana how they learn best, schedule sessions both can join with captions on, and have each run part of the work while Folasade reviews.
Ask Folasade to write a detailed step-by-step guide in her last two weeks, since a written guide works for everyone whatever their schedule or hearing.
Keep the shadowing plan as it is, and send Kwame and Ana Folasade's notes from any sessions or calls they could not fully join or follow.
feedback: This asks what the learners need, revises the schedule and provides practice with review. Confirm that the captioning and other agreed supports actually meet their needs; turning captions on alone does not establish access.
A guide is useful, but Folasade's phone judgment will not all reach the page, and nobody will have practiced the work before she goes. Kwame and Ana carry that gap alone.
Notes help, but Kwame and Ana would learn second-hand while others learn by doing. The plan was built around one way of working, and they bear the cost of that.
lessons.reflection: What do you know about your work that you have never written down? What would make it easier for someone whose needs differ from yours to learn it?
lessons.action: Choose a task that is appropriate for supervised practice. Agree on access, support and safeguards before a colleague tries it. Ask them to explain the steps and decisions, then update the guide together where the instructions were unclear.

check.question: For an authorized routine practice task, with agreed tools and accommodations available, which sign gives the best evidence that the handoff worked?
check.correct: The learner does the task and explains its key decisions without help.
wrong: A complete written guide has been saved in the team's shared folder.
The learner has shadowed the expert for all of the planned hours.
check.feedback: Demonstrating the work and explaining decisions gives direct evidence for this task. “Without help” here means without the expert supplying the answers; it does not exclude assistive technology, approved guides, accommodations or required oversight.

lessons.title: Reverse mentoring with clear boundaries and support
objectives: Explain what reverse mentoring is and what a leader can learn from a less senior colleague.
Plan a reverse mentoring pairing with clear goals, a written agreement and a way to end it.
Identify the risks the less senior partner carries and practical ways to reduce them.
Describe how to credit the mentor's time and knowledge as real work.
lessons.teaching:
In reverse mentoring, a more senior person learns from someone less senior. OPM's Best Practices: Mentoring guide describes it as a person junior in age, experience or position mentoring a senior one, and says success depends on openness and on setting aside barriers of status, power and position. The guide framed it around technology. Leaders now also use it to learn how instructions, meetings and processes land for people earlier in their careers or from different backgrounds. A newer colleague may see which instructions confuse new staff, how a process feels to the people it serves, or which tools would save time.

The evidence on reverse mentoring is still thin. Much of the research on reverse mentoring is qualitative, drawn from interviews and accounts of single programs. A 2019 review by Clarke and colleagues found little research in health sciences, and Patrice Gordon's 2025 overview calls the research largely qualitative. Treat it as a promising practice to try with care and review, not a proven program. A good account from one organization does not show what will happen in yours, so decide in advance what you hope to learn and check whether it happened.

The less senior partner may face particular risks when speaking candidly to someone who has organizational influence. Design the arrangement to reduce those risks without promising to eliminate them. Clarke and colleagues note that junior mentors may lack confidence, which can limit what gets said, and they stress mutual respect and reciprocity. Gordon stresses psychological safety, clear objectives and preparing both partners. In practice, keep it voluntary. This course recommends a pairing outside the leader’s chain of command to reduce conflicts. OPM’s federal mentoring guide identifies possible conflicts within that chain; it does not create a Minnesota-wide rule. Agree on roles, meeting frequency, privacy expectations and an exit process, using OPM’s agreement topics as a starting point. Explain applicable reporting and records duties before sensitive information is shared. A mentoring agreement cannot override those duties or guarantee secrecy.

Credit the mentor's knowledge as work. Gordon says mentees should value what mentors give, including their time, their knowledge and the emotional effort of speaking candidly to someone senior. Agree the time with the mentor's supervisor so it counts in their workload. When you act on what you learned, say where it came from, with the mentor's permission. Do not ask one person to speak for a whole group. Use this voluntary mentoring arrangement for learning rather than an undisclosed assessment of the mentor. Explain any authorized program records and evaluation in advance. If a disclosure triggers a reporting or records duty, follow that duty and the relevant protections.
lessons.keyPoint: Reverse mentoring can offer a different view of the work. Agree on goals, workload, privacy limits and a voluntary exit, and review what the arrangement helps each person learn.
lessons.example: Practice case: Kofi, a deputy director in the division, wants to understand how newer provider relations staff experience the licensing guidance his area publishes. He has asked Erik, a program consultant in his second year who reports to him two levels down, to be his reverse mentor. Erik agreed in the hallway but seemed hesitant. Kofi's assistant suggests announcing the pairing at the next all-staff meeting as a sign of openness. Kofi has not yet planned the first meeting.
lessons.question: What should Kofi do before the first meeting?
choices: Announce the pairing at the all-staff meeting, since visible support from a deputy director shows Erik's views are valued and may encourage others.
Keep the pairing private and informal, meeting whenever schedules allow, so that Erik feels no pressure and nothing has to be written down.
Check privately that Erik wants this, offer to pair with someone outside his reporting line instead, and agree goals, confidentiality and a way out.
feedback: Public support can matter, but announcing it before Erik has freely agreed makes it hard for him to decline and puts his name on a role he has not shaped.
An informal arrangement does not necessarily reduce pressure. Without agreed goals, workload arrangements and a clear exit, Erik may remain uncertain about what is expected and how to decline.

This checks Erik’s wishes, offers an option outside the reporting line and clarifies expectations. Explain the limits of confidentiality and any reporting duties as part of that agreement; the arrangement reduces risks but cannot guarantee safety.
lessons.reflection: When did you last learn something important about your work from someone less senior than you? What made it possible for them to tell you?
lessons.action: Write down two questions about your area's work that someone earlier in their career could answer better than you. Then ask your supervisor, or whoever coordinates mentoring in your area, how a voluntary pairing outside your reporting line could work.

check.question: Among these choices, which design best reduces pressure on the less senior partner in this voluntary reverse-mentoring arrangement?
check.correct: It is voluntary, outside their reporting line, with an agreed way to end it.
wrong: It is announced widely so all staff see that the leader backs the mentor.
The senior leader sets the goals, since they carry more responsibility.
check.feedback: Voluntary participation, distance from the reporting line and a clear exit can reduce pressure. They do not guarantee candor or remove reporting duties. An announcement or leader-set goals should not substitute for the mentor’s informed agreement.

lessons.title: Learning both ways across generations and difference
objectives: Apply questions that open two-way learning across generations, backgrounds and disability.
Compare how a knowledge exchange looks as a Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation practice.
Explain why generational labels are a weak basis for deciding who learns or teaches what.
Separate continuity notes about functions and knowledge from notes about individual people.
lessons.teaching:
Two-way learning makes room for knowledge held at different levels of experience. A colleague may contribute history, technical skill, a question about confusing instructions or an account of an access barrier. Ask what each person knows and wants to contribute instead of assigning expertise or perspective by age, tenure, background or disability. Start with your own defaults: what am I treating as the normal way to do this work, and where did I learn it?

Be careful with generational labels. A 2020 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report found the evidence for generational differences in work values weak and recommended attending to individual needs instead. Set aside ideas such as younger people being good with technology or longtime staff resisting change, and ask each person what they know and want to learn. Minnesota Management and Budget's retention guidance calls for succession planning that includes people with disabilities in the paths they are interested in. In practice that means asking each person what paths interest them, and making sure colleagues with disabilities are asked too.

The intercultural continuum shows how a learning practice can grow. IDI, LLC's Intercultural Development Continuum names five orientations: Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. A Minimization habit sounds like: we are all professionals, so I teach it the way I learned it. An Acceptance habit notices that generation, background and disability shape what people see and need. An Adaptation habit changes the exchange itself, with questions shared in advance, written and spoken ways to contribute, and newer staff leading a topic. These are program-created illustrations of the orientations, not assessments. One behavior does not establish a person’s place on the continuum. Ask about actual experience and access needs rather than inferring them from a group identity.

Keep the voluntary mentoring arrangement distinct from assigned work, required training and ordinary knowledge-sharing responsibilities. Participants can decline personal disclosure and use the agreed exit process. This does not remove job duties or the agency’s authority to arrange necessary training. Keep this learning exercise focused on functions and processes; maintain authorized assignment, training and personnel records through the relevant procedures. Review what changed, who could participate and what support is still needed. Use the responsible decision makers and applicable agency process for selection or duty changes.
lessons.keyPoint: Two-way learning grows when you question your own defaults, ask people rather than rely on generational labels, and adapt the exchange so everyone can contribute, while notes stay about functions.
lessons.example: Practice case: Rosa, who has ADHD and plans her own work around written agendas, supervises staff who work with lead agencies across the state. She runs a monthly knowledge exchange where experienced staff walk newer staff through the history of case review guidance. Newer staff rarely speak. Malik, a newer consultant who once worked in direct support, tells Rosa privately that he has ideas about how lead agencies read the guidance, but the sessions feel like a time to listen. Gloria, a manager, suggests Rosa track who contributes each month.
lessons.question: What should Rosa change first?
choices: Start a simple sheet of who speaks each month, so she can see the pattern and follow up with quieter staff one at a time.
Share questions ahead, invite a newer colleague to lead one topic each month, offer written input, and review the format with the group.
Ask Malik to present his ideas at the next session, since he raised them and his direct support experience is valuable to the whole team.
feedback: Tracking who speaks does not establish why participation differs or fix the format Malik described. Start by testing a more accessible exchange. Any individual participation record needs a legitimate purpose and appropriate handling; the problem is not merely that a record names someone.
This is the recommended choice. It changes the routine so different people can contribute in different ways, and it asks the group whether the change worked.
Malik's ideas may be useful, but singling him out after a private conversation puts him on the spot and leaves the format as it is for everyone else who stays quiet.
lessons.reflection: What did you learn about how work should be done from the people who trained you? Which of those habits would you now teach differently?
lessons.action: Choose a critical function and review its steps with the people who do it. Plan appropriate backup coverage, agree on support for learning, and invite a colleague new to the task to identify unclear instructions.

check.question: In this course’s illustrative continuum examples, which practice reflects an Adaptation approach to a knowledge exchange?
check.correct: Changing the format so people with different needs and experience can contribute.
wrong: Teaching everyone the same way, since good professionals need the same skills.
Noting which staff seem open to difference so leaders can pair them carefully.
check.feedback: This example changes the exchange in response to different needs. A uniform format can miss barriers, while impressions of a person’s openness are not an assessment of their developmental orientation.

cards.back: A look at a function that must keep working: its steps, decisions, contacts and documents, and how many people could do it. It names no successor.
A function whose practical knowledge is concentrated in one person. Review coverage and access to learning before an absence or transition creates a gap.
Practical knowledge that may not yet be explicit, such as the reasoning behind a decision. Observation, guided practice and discussion can help people explain and document it.
A learning relationship in which a more senior person learns from someone less senior. Agree on goals, workload, privacy limits and a voluntary exit; review whether it is useful.
An agreement about roles, goals, meeting frequency, privacy limits and ending the pairing. It must remain consistent with applicable reporting and records duties.

aid.heading: Reviewing a function for continuity
items: Name the function, not a person, and say why it must keep working.
List its steps, decisions, contacts and documents.
Count how many people could do it next month.
Ask who has had a chance to learn it and who has asked to.
Use the authorized agency process for vacancies, acting roles and duty changes, consulting Human Resources or labor relations as needed.

aid.heading: Sharing knowledge so everyone can learn
items: Ask learners what they need, then use captions, clear headings and plain language.
Move from watching, to working side by side, to doing with review.
Have the learner write or update the guide in their own words.
Share questions ahead, offer written and spoken ways to contribute, and invite newer staff to lead a topic.
Check the handoff through authorized practice, with relevant tools, accommodations and required supervision.

aid.heading: Setting up reverse mentoring
items: Confirm privately that the less senior partner wants to take part.
Choose a mentor who is not in the leader's own chain of command.
Agree goals, meeting frequency, privacy limits, reporting duties and an exit process.
Count the mentor's time as work and credit what you learn, with permission.
Keep this learning exercise focused on functions. Handle required individual or program records through authorized procedures.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Succession Planning Process (2005)
sources.note: Adapted from OPM's steps: finding real continuity issues, planning for long-term needs rather than position replacement, talent pools from several levels, and methods such as shadowing and communities of practice. Federal and dated.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Best Practices: Mentoring (2008)
sources.note: Adapted from OPM's definition of reverse mentoring and its point about status and power, knowledge transfer as a reason for mentoring, matching outside the chain of command, and mentoring agreement items. Federal and dated.

sources.title: Clarke, Burgess, van Diggele and Mellis — The role of reverse mentoring in medical education: current insights, Advances in Medical Education and Practice (2019)
sources.note: Supports the statements that research on reverse mentoring is limited, that junior mentors may lack confidence, and that mutual respect and reciprocity matter. An Australian review in medical education, not human services.

sources.title: Gordon, P. — Reverse Mentoring: Transforming Learning at Individual, Team, and Organizational Levels to Build Belonging in the Workplace, International Journal of HRD (2025)
sources.note: Supports the points that reverse mentoring research is largely qualitative and that psychological safety, clear objectives, preparing both partners and valuing mentors' time matter. A UK practitioner's perspective article.

sources.title: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine — Are Generational Categories Meaningful Distinctions for Workforce Management? (Summary, 2020)
sources.note: Supports the statement that evidence for generational differences in work values is weak and the advice to attend to individual needs instead. A national consensus report on the United States workforce.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Retention (Executive Order 19-15 resources)
sources.note: Supports the statement that succession planning should include a strategy to recruit and retain people with disabilities for the positions and career paths they are interested in. State executive branch guidance.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Supports orientation names and descriptions. The knowledge-exchange examples are the program’s illustrations; they do not assess a person or establish a developmental placement.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1433, ADA Reasonable Accommodation
sources.note: Supports recognizing requests without special wording and prompt referral to the appropriate decision maker.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation Policy
sources.note: Supports reporting duties that a mentoring agreement cannot waive. Confirm current contacts through DHS procedures.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Supports supervisors’ immediate reporting obligations under agency procedures.
